title: Gargi's questions in Janaka's court
hookLine: a king pays for an argument, and a woman asks the hardest questions in the room
carry: reasoned inquiry is the lamp of all learning
tomorrow: the whole science, it says, is one victory. over whom?

lines: A THOUSAND COWS FOR THE WISEST.
SHE COMES BACK WITH TWO ARROWS.
cards: King Janaka of Videha holds a great sacrifice and sets out a prize: a thousand cows with gold tied to their horns, for the most learned person in the room.
The sage Yajnavalkya simply tells his student to drive the cows home. Uproar. The scholars line up to test him, one after another.

Then Gargi Vachaknavi stands. She asks what everything is woven on, then what that is woven on, and keeps pushing, until Yajnavalkya warns her: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. She sits.
Later she stands again, asks the assembly's leave, and fires two more questions, like arrows.

teach.h: A COURT THAT PAYS FOR ARGUMENT.
teach.b: This is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and look at what it keeps. A king's court that pays for argument. A woman who presses the greatest sage in the land, and comes back for more.
When she's done, she tells the scholars plainly that none of them will beat him in debate about Brahman.
Hindu tradition has a name for formal argument over the texts, shastrartha, and it never stopped: schools answer schools, and many teachers take a sharp question as respect.
The Arthashastra, this week's handbook on power, builds that respect into a ruler's training.
It names four sciences: anvikshiki, reasoned inquiry; the Vedas; varta, farming, cattle and trade; and dandaniti, government.
It even lets rival schools speak first: one counts three sciences, one two, and one only government, because every other learning depends on order.

teach.h: RIVALS FIRST, THEN ANVIKSHIKI: THE LAMP OF ALL SCIENCES.
teach.b: Then it keeps all four and crowns reasoned inquiry, in paraphrase, the lamp of all sciences, the means of all action, the support of all dharma. It keeps the mind steady in good times and bad. That's the teaching.

teach.h: ASKING IS PART OF THE FAITH.
teach.b: In this tradition, asking is part of the faith, not a threat to it, and a king who wants to rule well puts questions at the center of his court.

how: Hindu scholars and schools still hold shastrartha, formal debate over the texts, and many study sessions open with the peace prayer saha navavatu, asking that teacher and student learn together without quarrel.

games.q: at temple youth class you ask why we offer food to the gods before we eat it. an aunty says 'don't question.' by Gargi's story, what's the hindu way?
o: ask, with respect. questions sit at the heart of the tradition.
stay quiet. in hinduism a good student never asks why.
argue until you win. that's what Gargi did.
games.why: Gargi asked, sat when warned, and came back with the assembly's leave. the Upanishads are full of questions, and the Arthashastra calls reasoned inquiry the lamp. asking, with respect, is the tradition.

practice: Many Hindu study sessions open with an old peace prayer, saha navavatu: may we be protected together, may our learning shine, may we never quarrel. If you pray, say it, or its meaning, quietly.
If you don't, bring to mind one question you've been afraid to ask, and hold it gently while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: The Arthashastra's opening: anvikshiki, reasoned inquiry, which it calls the lamp of all the sciences.

carryVoice: For the road: reasoned inquiry is the lamp of all learning. Gargi held it up in a king's court. Day fifteen eighty-five.
